[IBNHIBBAN:v8p101#2/r1] IBNHIBBAN, d. 354 · جرير بن عبد الله | reports | When destitute men arrived, the Prophet urged charity by reciting 4:1 and 59:18; an Anṣari's gift prompted others to give, and the Prophet taught that initiators of good or bad practice share its reward or burden and that of followers. | mentions 59:18
[IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p118#2/r1] IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA, d. 370 · author | reports | The Basran objection says an overt noun cannot coordinate with a genitive pronoun unless the preposition is repeated, since the pronoun and its preposition form one unit.
[IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p118#2/r2] IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA, d. 370 · author | reports | The Basrans also appeal to the rule against coordinating an unemphasized noun with a raised pronoun and to the Prophetic prohibition on swearing by anyone besides God.
[IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p118#2/r3] IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA, d. 370 · البصريون | rejects | The Basrans reject treating the genitive as poetic license because the Qur'an contains no place of metrical necessity.
[IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p118#2/r4] IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA, d. 370 · الكوفيون | reports | The Kufans permit the genitive by supplying an omitted preposition, and support the reader on that analysis.
[IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p118#2/r5] IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA, d. 370 · العجاج | reports | Al-ʿAjjāj's answer خير means بخير, illustrating an omitted preposition in ordinary speech.
[IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p118#2/r6] IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA, d. 370 · author | reports | A cited poetic line supplies another example of an omitted preposition: its opening رسم is understood as ورب رسم.
[IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p118#2/r7] IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA, d. 370 · بعضهم | reports | Another interpretation is to fear God regarding kinship ties, by not severing them.
[IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p118#2/r8] IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA, d. 370 · الكوفيون | prefers | Although the Kufans allow and defend the genitive, they still choose the accusative reading.
[IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p118/r4] IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA, d. 370 · author | holds | The light reading of تساءلون drops one of the two tāʾs from تتساءلون; the geminated reading assimilates the second tāʾ into sīn.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v3p118#3/r1] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · ابن كثير ونافع وابن عامر | reports | Ibn Kathīr, Nāfiʿ, and Ibn ʿĀmir read تساءلون with the first sīn doubled.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v3p118#3/r2] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · عاصم وحمزة والكسائي | reports | ʿĀṣim, Ḥamza, and al-Kisāʾī read تساءلون with a light sīn.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v3p118#3/r3] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · علي بن نصر وهارون بن موسى وعبيد بن عقيل وعبد الوهاب بن عطاء | reports | These transmitters report Abū ʿAmr reading the form lightly; al-Wāqidī via ʿAdī ibn al-Faḍl and Khārija ibn Muṣʿab also transmit the light form.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v3p118#3/r4] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · اليزيدي وعبد الوارث | reports | Al-Yazīdī and ʿAbd al-Wārith transmit the doubled form from Abū ʿAmr; Abū Zayd reports both, while ʿAbbās permits either but says Abū ʿAmr reads lightly.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v3p118#3/r5] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | The doubled form comes from تتساءلون, with tāʾ assimilated to sīn because they share articulation near the tongue-tip and upper incisors and are both voiceless.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v3p118#3/r6] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | The light form drops one tāʾ from تتفاعلون because adjacent similar consonants are eased by deletion; such clusters can also be eased through assimilation or substitution.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v3p118#3/r7] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | reports | The word طست illustrates substitution of a second sīn with tāʾ because of their closeness and shared voicelessness; al-ʿAjjāj's line is cited for طست.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v3p118#3/r8] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو عثمان | reports | Abū ʿUthmān cites a verse whose final word الطس illustrates the same consonant pattern.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v3p121/r1] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · حمزة | reports | Ḥamza reads والأرحام in the genitive; the other readers read it in the accusative.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v3p121/r2] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | The accusative can coordinate with the syntactic position of the prepositional phrase, or with واتقوا, meaning to honor kinship ties and not sever them.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v3p121/r3] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | rejects | The genitive reading coordinates الأرحام with the pronoun governed by bāʾ; Abū ʿAlī considers this weak in analogy and rare in usage, so prefers avoiding it.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v3p121/r4] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | A bound pronoun replaces tanwīn and is too closely attached to its noun for a ظاهر noun to coordinate with it, unlike a visible genitive complement that can be separated by an adverb.
[IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v1p179/r1] IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB, d. 392 · أبو عبد الرحمن عبد الله بن يزيد | reports | Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ʿAbd Allāh ibn Yazīd reads والأرحام in the nominative.
[IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v1p179/r2] IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB, d. 392 · author | holds | He parses nominative الأرحام as a topic with an omitted predicate: the kinship ties are also something people must revere and protect; this raises their emphasis above an accusative or genitive adjunct.
[IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v1p179/r3] IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB, d. 392 · author | holds | An omitted predicate is recoverable from context, whereas deleting an accusative or genitive الأرحام would leave no indication that kinship ties were intended; raising the phrase emphasizes it, as in al-Farazdaq’s complaint.
[IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v1p179/r4] IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB, d. 392 · author | reports | A separate semantic explanation of the raised poetic phrase treats both coordinated descriptions as remaining after the speaker called only for one of them.

[SULAMI:v1p138#2/r4] SULAMI, d. 412 · بعضهم | reports | One view defines piety as abandoning every act of opposition to God.
[SULAMI:v1p138#2/r5] SULAMI, d. 412 · سهل | reports | Sahl says piety requires leaving every sin and anything that brings a fault, including forbidden acts and indecencies.
[SULAMI:v1p138#2/r6] SULAMI, d. 412 · بعضهم | reports | One view identifies piety with following the Prophet.
[SULAMI:v1p138#2/r7] SULAMI, d. 412 · بعضهم | reports | One view says piety in commands is avoiding delay, in prohibitions resisting desire, in exhortation keeping noble manners, in encouragement concealing one's inner state, and in threats not persisting in ignorance.
[SULAMI:v1p138#2/r8] SULAMI, d. 412 · بعضهم | reports | One view defines piety from God as avoiding everything besides God.
[SULAMI:v1p138#2/r9] SULAMI, d. 412 · الجريري | reports | Al-Jurayri says without piety and vigilance in one's relation to God, one cannot attain unveiling and direct vision.

[THALABI:v3p241#2/r1] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | The single soul is Adam, and the spouse created from it is Eve; the commentary points to parallel wording in al-Aʿrāf and al-Zumar. | mentions 7:189, 39:6

[THALABI:v3p241#2/r3] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | تسائلون به means that people ask one another by God; the Kūfans lighten it by dropping one of the two tāʾs, as in the prohibition ولا تعاونوا. | mentions 5:2
[THALABI:v3p241#2/r4] THALABI, d. 427 · قراءة العامة | reports | The standard reading puts الأرحام in the accusative, coordinated with اتقوا: fear God and do not sever family ties.
[THALABI:v3p241#2/r5] THALABI, d. 427 · النخعي ويحيى بن وثاب وطلحة بن مصرف وقتادة والأعمش وحمزة | reports | These readers put الأرحام in the genitive, coordinating it with the pronoun governed by bi and reading the appeal as by God and by kinship.
[THALABI:v3p241#2/r6] THALABI, d. 427 · author | prefers | The accusative is more correct and eloquent: Arabic normally does not coordinate an explicit noun to the meaning of a preposition without repeating that preposition or using the accusative, though poetry permits the construction.
[THALABI:v3p241#2/r7] THALABI, d. 427 · شاعر | reports | An unattributed poetic example is cited as evidence that this construction can occur in poetry.
[THALABI:v3p241#2/r8] THALABI, d. 427 · شاعر | reports | A second unattributed line offers another poetic instance of the construction with والأيام.
[THALABI:v3p242/r1] THALABI, d. 427 · عبد الله بن يزيد المقبري | reports | He recites al-arham in the nominative, either as a new subject after the preceding clause or as an exhortation; Arabs may raise an exhortative noun.
[THALABI:v3p242/r2] THALABI, d. 427 · الفراء | reports | Al-Farra cites a poem illustrating Arabic use of the nominative for an exhortation, with the repeated call to arms.
[THALABI:v3p242/r3] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | Raqīb means guardian or watchful keeper and may carry the active sense of faʿil.

[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p446#2/r1] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | holds | The one soul is Adam; this origin is a favor because common descent should bring people closer to mutual affection.

[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p446#2/r3] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | reports | One view specifies the left rib, which explains the saying that woman is a crooked rib.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p446#2/r4] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · النبي | reports | A report from the Prophet at the verse's revelation says woman was created from man, whose concern is woman, while man's concern is clay.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p446#2/r5] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · مجاهد | reports | Mujahid and Ibrahim understand asking through God and kinship as the formula “I ask you by God and by kin”; Hamza reads al-arham in the genitive on this interpretation.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p446#2/r6] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · قتادة | reports | Qatada and al-Suddi instead read the phrase as a command to maintain kinship and not sever it; the opening's common origin means people are siblings, even when distant.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p446#2/r7] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · مجاهد | reports | Mujahid explains raqib as a guardian or preserver.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p446#2/r8] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · ابن زيد | reports | Ibn Zayd explains raqib as knowing or all-aware.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p193/r1] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | reports | Some derive the word name from elevation and others from a mark; both derivations support inward readings.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p193/r10] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | reports | Whoever forgets the Real has no end to tribulation, while whoever forgets creation has no end to spiritual elevation.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p193/r11] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | reports | God calls sinners who forgot His covenant, rejected His love, and exceeded His limits back to His door to receive gentleness and favor.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p193/r12] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | reports | God tells the knowers who forgot their own share in Him and turned from all else that their right, support, and rank have become great with Him.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p193/r13] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | reports | One who delights in the breeze of nearness, rests in witnessing God's face, and gains honor from His majesty is the most honored servant.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p193/r14] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | holds | Taqwa encompasses all obedience, beginning with avoiding associationism and culminating in avoiding every other-than-God; the first other is one's own self.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p193/r15] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | holds | One who guards against the self stands with God without claiming a station or witnessing a spiritual state.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p193/r2] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | holds | Under the elevation derivation, remembering God raises one's rank, knowing Him raises one's state, and companionship with Him raises one's aspiration; these bring abundant rewards, inward lights, and escape from base attachments.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p193/r3] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | holds | Under the mark derivation, seeking God marks one with worship, companionship with intention, love with the mark of the elect, and knowledge with the mark of the chosen.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p193/r4] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | holds | The worshipper's mark protects from the fire, the seeker is too honored for the Garden to enslave him, and the elect's mark removes self-conceit about deserving closeness.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p193/r5] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | holds | The mark of the special ones is the heart's grief of separation; union with God elevates His rank beyond imagining, while distance brands the heart with separation.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p193/r6] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | holds | The word people is a collective noun, and its derivation is not strong.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p193/r7] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | reports | It is said that insan derives from visibility; inwardly, people appeared from nonexistence under obligation, while God honors some with knowledge and guidance and disposes of all as He wills.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p193/r8] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | reports | It is said God brought people forth from nonexistence as their likenesses and disclosed to no one else the states He disclosed to them.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p193/r9] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | reports | It is said insan derives from forgetfulness: forgetting God is the lowest condition and forgetting His remembrance the most abased state.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p194/r1] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | holds | The one who stands for God does so without seeking a share in this world or the next.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p194/r10] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | holds | Knowing that God watches over someone should make that person ashamed before Him.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p194/r11] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | holds | God litigates against a caretaker who violates those in his care and avenges servants more than He avenges Himself; a just and kind orphan guardian has a claim with God, while an abusive one faces God as adversary.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p194/r2] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | holds | The one soul is Adam; since he was created by God's hand, those descended from him share this distinction and are the best of creation. | mentions 98:7
[QUSHAYRI:v1p194/r3] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | holds | The word soul is generic, and its generic sense implies exhaustive inclusion.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p194/r4] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | holds | God made creatures dwell with one another so lineage could continue and like could return to like by pairing form with form.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p194/r5] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | holds | Creating all humanity from one person despite their varied bodies, appearances, characters, aspirations, and conditions proves God's power, lordship, and wisdom.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p194/r6] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | holds | No two people resemble one another in appearance, character, aspiration, and condition, demonstrating the limitless scope of God's power and knowledge.

[TABRISI:4:1#2/r6] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Both forms are used in the language for spreading a secret: بثثتك سري and أبثثتك سري.
[TABRISI:4:1#2/r7] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | رقيب comes from watching and waiting; it means a guardian from whom nothing is hidden, while رقبي describes each person awaiting the other’s death.

[TABRISI:4:1#2/r9] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | reports | One view says prior scriptures addressed people as the poor, while the Quran uses يا أيها الناس in Meccan revelation and addresses either believers or all people in Medinan revelation.

[TABRISI:4:1#3/r10] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | On that reading, as people honor God in their words, they should honor Him through obedience.

[TABRISI:4:1#3/r12] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | On this second reading, al-arḥām is accusative and coordinated with God's name; the construction supports a duty to maintain kinship ties.

[TABRISI:4:1#3/r14] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Maintaining kinship can mean accepting one's lineage, giving financial support to relatives, and similar acts.

[TABRISI:4:1#3/r17] TABRISI, d. 548 · ابن زيد | reports | Ibn Zayd explains raqīb as one who knows; the author says this and the guardian sense are close.
[TABRISI:4:1#3/r18] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Kana indicates God's continuing vigilance from Adam through the addressed generation; He knows all that they do and nothing escapes Him.

[TABRISI:4:1/r10] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Unlike a pronoun, an overt noun can be separated from its genitive by an adverb or other material, making the two forms less alike.
[TABRISI:4:1/r11] TABRISI, d. 548 · سيبويه | reports | Sibawayh cites a poem coordinating الأيام with the genitive pronoun بك, an example of poetic license.
[TABRISI:4:1/r2] TABRISI, d. 548 · الباقون | reports | The remaining readers geminate the sin in تسألون.
[TABRISI:4:1/r3] TABRISI, d. 548 · حمزة | reports | Hamza reads الأرحام in the genitive.
[TABRISI:4:1/r4] TABRISI, d. 548 · الباقون | reports | The remaining readers use the accusative for الأرحام.

[TABRISI:4:1/r6] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | The light reading contracts تتساءلون by deleting a ta where similar letters come together; the geminated reading merges ta into sin, helped by their shared articulation and voicelessness.
[TABRISI:4:1/r7] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | The accusative الأرحام can coordinate either with the object governed by the preposition or with اتقوا, yielding a command to maintain kinship ties.
[TABRISI:4:1/r8] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | The genitive reading coordinates the noun with the pronoun governed by باء, a construction weak by analogy and rare in usage.
[TABRISI:4:1/r9] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | The attached pronoun resembles tanwin because each is a single silent element that cannot be separated from its noun; the analogy is supported by dropping the ya in vocative forms such as يا غلام.
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p219/r8] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · أهل التفسير | reports | Taqwā can mean fear or reverence; Noah, Hūd, Ṣāliḥ, and Shuʿayb use it in exhortations to their people. | mentions 26:106, 26:124, 26:142, 26:177

[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p310/r6] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · أهل التفسير | reports | Raqib can mean one who waits, as in 11:93 and 44:59. | mentions 11:93, 44:59
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p594#2/r12] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · بعض المفسرين | reports | One Qur'anic sense of nafs is Adam, from whom humanity was created.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v2p1/r1] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · عطية عن ابن عباس، الحسن، مجاهد، جابر بن زيد، قتادة | reports | One view says this verse was revealed in Mecca; it is transmitted by Atiyya from Ibn Abbas and held by Hasan, Mujahid, Jabir ibn Zayd, and Qatada.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v2p1/r10] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · كعب الأحبار ووهب وابن إسحاق | reports | Another report says Eve was created before Adam entered the Garden.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v2p1/r11] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas relates that God put Adam to sleep and created Eve from his left rib without causing him pain; after waking, Adam identified her as Hawwaʾ.

[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v2p1/r3] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · الماوردي | reports | A qualified view says the sura is Medinan except 4:58, revealed at Mecca when Muhammad sought the Kaaba keys from Uthman ibn Talha to give them to al-Abbas. | mentions 4:58
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v2p1/r4] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · ابن عباس | reports | The command to be mindful of the Lord means obedience.

[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v2p1/r9] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · ابن مسعود وابن عباس | reports | One report says Eve was created after Adam entered the Garden.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v2p2/r1] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · الفراء | holds | Baththa means to spread; Arabs also say abaththa for God spreading creation and use the verb for disclosing what is within oneself.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v2p2/r10] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · الزجاج | rejects | Al-Zajjaj rejects the genitive grammatically except in poetic necessity and theologically because the Prophet forbade swearing by fathers.

[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v2p2/r13] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · أبو علي | prefers | Abu Ali parses the genitive as coordinated with the pronoun governed by bi, but calls it weak and rare, so avoiding it is better.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v2p2/r14] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · ابن عباس ومجاهد | reports | Al-raqīb means the guardian or keeper, according to Ibn Abbas and Mujahid.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v2p2/r15] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · الخطابي | reports | Al-Khattabi describes al-raqīb as a guardian from whom nothing is absent; among people it is one assigned to protect something vigilantly without heedlessness.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v2p2/r2] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | reports | A number of named readers and transmitters read tasaʾalūn with a doubled sīn; other listed readers and transmitters read it lightly.

[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v2p2/r7] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · الزجاج | reports | A third interpretation is that people seek their rights by invoking God.

[RAZI-FULL:v9p128/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The surah centers on duties of compassion and rights toward children, women, and orphans, returns to this theme at its end, and also prescribes purification, prayer, and fighting; its burdensome duties open by grounding taqwa in God's creation. | mentions 4:176
[RAZI-FULL:v9p128/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas, as transmitted by al-Wahidi, takes the address يا أيها الناس to refer to the people of Mecca.

[RAZI-FULL:v9p128/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The definite plural الناس denotes all people, supporting the general address.
[RAZI-FULL:v9p128/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The command to fear God is justified by creation from one soul, a rationale shared by all humanity descended from Adam.
[RAZI-FULL:v9p128/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Taqwa is required of everyone worldwide, not only Meccans, reinforcing the universal scope of the address and its rationale.

[RAZI-FULL:v9p129/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Since God alone is creator, deity, and lord, people must worship Him and avoid His prohibitions.
[RAZI-FULL:v9p129/r7] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | No obedience independently earns reward: the capacity and motive to obey come from God, making obedience itself a divine blessing rather than payment owed to the servant.
[RAZI-FULL:v9p130#2/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الأصم | reports | Al-Asamm says reason alone cannot show that humans had to descend from one soul; since an unlettered Prophet reported this unseen fact without a teacher, it proves prophecy, while خلقكم indicates knowledge of divine unity.

[RAZI-FULL:v9p130#2/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الشاعر | reports | An unnamed poet uses the feminine form of خليفة in a line about someone born as successor, offered as a parallel for grammatical agreement with النفس.
[RAZI-FULL:v9p130/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Humanity's descent from one person yields people of diverse colors, appearances, and builds, showing a freely acting creator rather than an influencing nature, and warrants obedience to His commands.
[RAZI-FULL:v9p130/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Shared origin from one soul should increase compassion among people, especially toward orphans, women, and the weak, because kinship creates intimacy and affection.
[RAZI-FULL:v9p130/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | The Prophet says Fatima is a part of him and whatever harms her harms him, illustrating the affection created by kinship.
[RAZI-FULL:v9p130/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Recognizing that everyone descends from one person should end boasting and arrogance and produce humility and good character.
[RAZI-FULL:v9p130/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The creation of diverse people from one person's loins and a drop of semen also proves resurrection: raising the dead should be no harder for God. | mentions 53:31
[RAZI-FULL:v9p131/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الأكثرون | reports | Most exegetes say the spouse is Eve, created from Adam's left rib while he slept; when he awoke he saw and was drawn to her as part of himself.
[RAZI-FULL:v9p131/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | A Prophetic report says woman was created from a crooked rib and that straightening it breaks it; leaving it crooked allows enjoyment of her.
[RAZI-FULL:v9p131/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · أبو مسلم الأصفهاني | reports | Abu Muslim al-Isfahani instead interprets منها as from the same kind, as in verses saying that spouses and a messenger are from among the people themselves. | mentions 16:72, 3:164, 9:128
[RAZI-FULL:v9p131/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · القاضي | prefers | Al-Qadi prefers the first view because if Eve were independently created, humanity would come from two souls; the author notes that min may instead mark the beginning of creation with Adam.
[RAZI-FULL:v9p131/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Even if God could create Eve from earth as He created Adam, the author asks what benefit there would be in creating her from Adam's rib.
[RAZI-FULL:v9p131/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas derives Adam's name from the earth's surface, whose varied colors and qualities are reflected among his descendants.
[RAZI-FULL:v9p131/r7] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | The commentary also explains Hawwa's name by saying that she was created from a living part of Adam, namely a rib.
[RAZI-FULL:v9p132#2/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الواحدي | reports | Al-Wahidi explains بث as dispersing and spreading people.

[RAZI-FULL:v9p132#2/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الفراء والزجاج | reports | Al-Farraʾ and al-Zajjaj note that some Arabs say أبث الله الخلق for God spread the creation.
[RAZI-FULL:v9p132#2/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Saying God spread men and women, rather than spreading men and women from both parents, avoids implying that Adam and Eve themselves were spread from themselves.
[RAZI-FULL:v9p132#2/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Only men are called numerous because their prominence makes their numbers more conspicuous; the wording signals men's visibility and women's concealment.
[RAZI-FULL:v9p132#2/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | Those who say humanity existed as particles in Adam's loins read the spreading literally; opponents understand it as Adam and Eve's offspring and later descendants, attributed to them figuratively.
[RAZI-FULL:v9p132/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · المتكلمون | rejects | The theologians reject the natural philosophers' claim that creation requires prior material: something either identical to prior matter was not created, or different from it arose from pure nonexistence.

[RAZI-FULL:v9p133#2/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | rejects | The author says these grammatical objections cannot outweigh transmitted linguistic usage: Hamza was one of the seven, and the reading is presumed to come from the Prophet, so hearing outweighs weak analogy.
[RAZI-FULL:v9p133#2/r10] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الشاعر | reports | An unnamed poet's phrase ولا الحديدا is cited as evidence for coordinating the accusative with a prepositional phrase's syntactic position.
[RAZI-FULL:v9p133#2/r11] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · مجاهد وقتادة والسدي والضحاك وابن زيد والفراء والزجاج | reports | The majority exegetical reading supplies a command to fear kinship by preserving ties and not severing them; the author says it proves severing kinship forbidden and maintaining ties obligatory.

[RAZI-FULL:v9p133#2/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | One defense of Hamza's genitive reading assumes the preposition is repeated: تساءلون به وبالأرحام.
[RAZI-FULL:v9p133#2/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · سيبويه | reports | Sibawayh cites an anonymous poem using وما بك والأيام as poetic evidence for the genitive coordination construction.

[BAYDAWI-FULL:4:1/r15] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | reports | A nominative reading treats al-arḥām as a subject with an omitted predicate: it too is something to be guarded or invoked by.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:4:1/r16] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | By pairing kinship with His honored name, God indicates that maintaining family ties is owed for His sake.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:4:1/r17] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · النبي | reports | A Prophetic report depicts kinship as suspended from the Throne, asking God to join whoever maintains it and sever whoever cuts it.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:4:1/r2] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | The one soul from which humanity was created is Adam.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:4:1/r3] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | His spouse was created from him: Eve was made from one of Adam’s ribs.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:4:1/r4] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | reports | Alternatively, an omitted clause means “from one soul He created, and from it He created its spouse,” reaffirming humanity’s single origin.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:4:1/r5] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | The spreading of many men and women explains how they descend from the original pair; the verse mentions many men without repeating “many” for women because wisdom requires women to be more numerous.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:4:1/r6] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | The masculine plural “many” follows the collective construction.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:4:1/r7] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | The origin story grounds the command to fear God in His overwhelming power and abundant blessing, which call for fear and obedience.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:4:1/r8] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | reports | Alternatively, the command prepares people for piety in the rights of household members and fellow human beings discussed in the following verses.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:4:1/r9] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | reports | A reading has khāliqun and bāththun with an omitted subject, estimated as “and He is creator and spreader.”
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p201#2/r1] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | The address to people means the children of Adam.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p201#2/r10] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | reports | Kufan readers use the lightened tasāʾalūn form by dropping the second tāʾ to avoid two consecutive tāʾs.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p201#2/r11] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | People ask one another by God and by kinship, appealing for a favor.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p201#2/r12] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | reports | Al-arḥām may be accusative, coordinated with God's name or with the syntactic position of the prepositional phrase, meaning people must not sever kinship ties.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p201#2/r13] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · حمزة | reports | Ḥamza reads al-arḥām in the genitive, coordinating the explicit noun with the attached pronoun; Nasafi calls this weak because the pronoun and prepositional phrase are tightly connected.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p201#2/r14] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | reports | Raqīb means either guardian or one who knows.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p201#2/r2] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | The one soul is Adam, the common origin from which God brought humankind forth.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p201#2/r3] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | The syntax implies that God first brought the one soul into being, then created its spouse from it; Eve was created from one of Adam's ribs.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p201#2/r4] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | God spread the two human sexes from Adam and Eve, detailing how humanity was created from them.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p201#2/r5] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | The address concerns those to whom the Messenger was sent: their origin is Adam and Eve, and countless earlier peoples also descended from them.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p201#2/r6] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | Mentioning creation after the command to fear God is fitting because the creation displays God's immense power, including power to punish unbelievers, and reflection on it should instill fear.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p201#2/r7] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | Creation is also an overwhelming favor, so people owe God fear and must not be ungrateful for it.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p201#2/r8] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | reports | At the verse's revelation, the Prophet said woman was created from man and is concerned with man, while man was created from earth and is concerned with earth.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p201#2/r9] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | The underlying form is tatasāʾalūn; the first tāʾ assimilates into sīn after being changed to sīn because the sounds are close and both unvoiced.
[QASHANI:4:1/r1] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | Fear God by not claiming His attributes for your good deeds; treat Him as your protection and recognize that good issues from the absolutely powerful.
[QASHANI:4:1/r10] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | Outward kinship images inner connection; the outward rule in unity reflects the inward one, so failure to honor outward kinship predicts failure to honor the inward.
[QASHANI:4:1/r11] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | God watches so that people do not become veiled by a manifested attribute or remnant of self and suffer its torment.
[QASHANI:4:1/r2] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | The single soul is the universal rational soul, the heart of the world and the real Adam.
[QASHANI:4:1/r3] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | The spouse is the animal soul that emerges from the rational soul.
[QASHANI:4:1/r4] QASHANI, d. 736 · قيل | reports | Another view says the spouse was created from Adam’s left rib on the side facing the created world; without her he would not have descended, and Satan used her to tempt him. Bodily attachment occurs only through her.
[QASHANI:4:1/r5] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | The many men are people of heart who incline toward their father, while women are people of soul and temperament who incline toward their mother.
[QASHANI:4:1/r6] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | Fear God in His essence by affirming no independent existence of your own, and make Him your protection when remnants of self appear during annihilation in unity, so they do not veil you.
[QASHANI:4:1/r7] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | The phrase “by whom you ask one another” means asking through God, not through yourselves.
[QASHANI:4:1/r8] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | The real wombs are relations to high principles, separate spirits, and the spirits of prophets and saints; cutting them by withholding love turns unity into separation and estranges one from God.
[QASHANI:4:1/r9] QASHANI, d. 736 · رسول الله | reports | The Prophet says that maintaining kinship increases lifespan, meaning it brings lasting subsistence.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p488/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Raqīb is an intensive form from raqaba: to watch an affair closely to ascertain its true state, with an associated sense of guarding; the passage lists watcher, arrow, snake, lookout, and waiting as related usages.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p488/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · أبو داود | reports | Abu Dawud’s cited verse uses الرقباء in describing watchers positioned in ambush, as lexical evidence for the watcher sense.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p492/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | Most scholars consider the surah Medinan, with a reported exception for the verse about returning trusts; al-Nahhas calls it Meccan, and al-Naqqash says it descended at the Migration, though all agree it includes Medinan material. | mentions 4:58
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p492/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | Al-Bukhari identifies the inheritance question about collateral relatives as the last verse revealed. | mentions 4:176
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p492/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The opening follows the prior surah’s account of communities and God’s promise not to waste anyone’s work by returning to the common human origin, encouraging concord, affection, and mutual care. | mentions 3:195
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p492/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The single-origin reminder argues for piety: the One able to create humanity in this remarkable way deserves to be obeyed and feared.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p492/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Mentioning one human origin appeals to natural affinity among kindred species and encourages people to unite in piety.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p492/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | prefers | Al-nās is general because of its definite article, and both the call to piety and its rationale apply generally.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p492/r8] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · قيل | reports | An alternative takes “people” as the Meccans, based on Arabs’ custom of pleading by God and kinship

[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p492/r9] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · قيل | reports | Another alternative takes “people” to mean the believers, in light of the statement that believers are brothers. | mentions 49:10
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p493/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | When a people-address includes disbelievers, the Qur'an often follows with proofs of divine unity and lordship; when it addresses believers, it often follows with reminders of blessings they already recognize. | mentions 22:7, 2:21
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p493/r10] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الأصم | reports | Al-Asamm says reason alone cannot establish that humanity was created from one self; that claim rests on transmitted revelation.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p493/r11] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The possessive link to Adam treats him as the source of later generations even though descendants arise through procreation; this counters materialist claims about humanity’s origin.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p493/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · قيل | reports | Some treat this opening as parallel to the opening of al-Hajj: this surah, fourth in the first half, grounds piety in human origin, while al-Hajj, fourth in the second half, grounds it in the afterlife. | mentions 22:1
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p493/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The first mention of piety is general avoidance of whatever brings punishment; another reading is specific piety in preserving people’s rights and maintaining their mutual ties.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p493/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas glosses piety as obedience.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p493/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · مقاتل | reports | Muqatil glosses piety as fear of God.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p493/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · قيل | reports | Another explanation defines piety as avoiding major and minor sins.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p493/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The single self is Adam.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p493/r8] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | The majority read واحدة with feminine agreement to nafs; Ibn Abi Abla reads واحد, matching the intended Adam or treating nafs as masculine.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p493/r9] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Creation here means originating through branching and returning to one source; the cited verse illustrates bodily descent from an origin.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p494/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Since Muhammad was unlettered and had not read scripture, creation’s complexity points to divine unity, while the single origin points to prophethood.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p494/r10] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن عباس وابن مسعود | reports | One report says Eve was created while Adam was in the Garden; another says she was made before his entry, as Kaab al-Ahbar, Wahb, and Ibn Ishaq hold.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p494/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The single origin discourages pride and rivalry and also indicates resurrection: the One who brought diverse people from one person can more readily revive them.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p494/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن عباس ومجاهد والسدي | reports | They identify Adam as the self from whom Eve, his wife, was initially created.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p494/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · قتادة | reports | Qatada says Adam slept alone in the Garden, and God made Eve from a short rib taken from his left side, or according to another report his right.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p494/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن عطية | reports | Ibn Atiyya cites the authentic hadith that woman was created from a crooked rib and that straightening it breaks it, glossed as divorce.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p494/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | Abu Hayyan allows a figurative reading of the rib: women’s changeable temperaments and difficult handling resemble a crooked rib, as humanity is described as hasty. | mentions 21:37
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p494/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن بحر وأبو مسلم | reports | Ibn Bahr and Abu Muslim say “from it” means from Adam’s kind, as in other verses saying spouses or a messenger are from among you. | mentions 16:72, 9:128
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p494/r8] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · القاضي | reports | The Judge prefers literal creation from Adam, reasoning that if Eve were independently created humanity would have two origins; Abu Hayyan answers that من can mark the starting point of creation.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p494/r9] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | Another view takes the pronoun in منها to refer to the clay separated from Adam’s clay, so Eve was made of the same material as Adam.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p495/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The coordinating wāw does not imply temporal order; Adam’s creation is mentioned first because the addressed people are the focus, as in the command to worship the Lord who created them and those before them. | mentions 2:21
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p495/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الزمخشري | reports | Zamakhshari posits an omitted earlier phrase so Eve’s creation follows Adam’s creation in time; Abu Hayyan says this grammatical workaround is unnecessary.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p495/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الزمخشري | reports | Zamakhshari also connects the phrase directly to “created you,” with Adam as the single self and Eve as the mother of those addressed; Abu Hayyan says this fits Arabic syntax.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p495/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | A further parsing connects “created her spouse” to the participle واحدَة, understood as “a self made single,” with خلق as “created” or “separated.”
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p495/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · قيل | reports | An unusual interpretation reads the single self as the spirit, its spouse as the body, and creation as their composition; Abu Hayyan says this differs from earlier commentators. | mentions 51:49, 36:36
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p495/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | rejects | Abu Hayyan says Zamakhshari’s ellipsis is unnecessary because the direct analysis already fits Arabic syntax.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p496#2/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن عطية | reports | Ibn Atiyya says the light reading deletes the second tāʾ of تتساءلون; Abu Hayyan notes the Kufan grammarian Hisham instead says it deletes the imperfect prefix tāʾ.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p496#2/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · أبو علي | reports | Abu Ali says adjacent sounds may be lightened through deletion, assimilation, or substitution, and cites طست from طس with an al-Ajjaj verse.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p496#2/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | rejects | Abu Hayyan says Ibn Atiyya should note that retention is original and assimilation is close to it; deletion follows identical consonants, not merely nearby sounds.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p496#2/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Assimilation is not confined to the tafaʿʿul form but occurs across several verb forms; deletion, however, is limited to imperfects beginning with the extra tāʾ.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p496#2/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | rejects | The claim that close sounds always trigger reduction is too broad; Abu Ali means only that reduction can occur, and طست is an example of doubled consonants instead.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p496#2/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | يتساءلون به means that people ask one another by God, including the formula “I ask you by God to do this,” or invoke God to emphasize their rights.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p496#2/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · عبد الله | reports | Ibn Masud reads with the simple verb تسألون, and another form drops the hamza and transfers its vowel to the sin.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p496#2/r8] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · طائفة | reports | A group says the phrase means invoking God to claim rights and treating Him as exalted.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p496/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | بث منهما means that God spread and dispersed humanity from Adam and his wife; Arabic also uses the quadriliteral أبث for this sense.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p496/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · قيل | reports | The indefinite رجال and the added كثيرا emphasize broad spread; men are mentioned first for their superiority, while the adjective “many” is understood with women as well.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p496/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · قيل | reports | Another explanation says the adjective is intentionally attached only to men because men publicly appear while women are meant to remain hidden.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p496/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · قيل | reports | The division into male and female is taken to mean there is no third sex; apparently ambiguous cases must ultimately belong to one of these two kinds.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p496/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | A variant reads وخالق منها زوجها as an active participle with an omitted subject, “and He is creating her spouse from it.”
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p496/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The repeated command to fear God reinforces the first, or distinguishes nurture and beneficence in “your Lord” from awe and threat in “God.” | mentions 32:16, 21:90
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p496/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | The majority read تساءلون; the Kufans lighten the sin, deriving it from the original تتساءلون.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p497/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن عباس وقتادة والسدي | reports | They parse الأرْحام accusative as “avoid cutting kinship ties,” with an omitted noun; piety toward God means obedience, while piety toward kin means maintaining ties through kindness.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p497/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The shared sense of avoiding violation reconciles the different applications and answers the objection that one word cannot carry different meanings; kinship’s coordination with God highlights the gravity of severing ties. | mentions 2:83

[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p497/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | Another accusative parse attaches الأرْحام to the implied object of the preposition به, supported by Ibn Masud’s reading with a repeated preposition.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p497/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | The nominative can begin a sentence with an omitted predicate: Ibn Atiyya supplies “kin deserve to be joined,” while Zamakhshari supplies that they are to be revered or invoked; Abu Hayyan prefers the latter as closer to the wording.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p497/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الحسن والنخعي ومجاهد | reports | They explain the genitive reading as coordination with the attached pronoun in به without repeating the preposition, supported by the reading وبالأرحام.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p497/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The wording also reflects people invoking God and kinship together when making appeals.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p498/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الزمخشري | reports | Zamakhshari rejects attaching الأرْحام to the bound pronoun without repeating the preposition, arguing that the pronoun and preposition form a tightly joined unit.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p498/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن عطية | reports | Ibn Atiyya says leading Basran grammarians disallow coordinating an overt noun with a genitive pronoun; Sibawayh permits it only in poetry, though some grammarians accept it.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p498/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | rejects | Abu Hayyan says al-Mazani’s analogy fails because رأيتك وزيدا is accepted although رأيت زيداوك is not.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p498/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن عطية | reports | Ibn Atiyya further argues that a genitive pronoun cannot separate from its preposition and therefore behaves like part of a word.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p499/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن عطية | reports | Ibn Atiyya objects that the genitive reading contributes no useful exhortation and implies swearing by kinship; he cites the prohibition on swearing by anything but God.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p499/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · قيل | reports | Some take the wāw as an oath particle rather than coordination, making the following clause the oath’s response and treating kinship as honored by God.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p499/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | prefers | Abu Hayyan endorses the Kufan rule permitting coordination to a genitive pronoun without repeating the preposition and rejects the Basran restriction as unsound. | mentions 2:217
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p499/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | rejects | He sharply rebukes Ibn Atiyya for rejecting a mutawatir reading transmitted from the Prophet through senior Companions and the leading reciters.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p499/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Abu Hayyan defends Hamza’s integrity and transmission, says readers need not follow Basran grammarians, and insists Arabic usage exceeds what any one school transmitted.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p500/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Allah’s being ever watchful is not restricted to past time; He continually observes and knows everything about people.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p531/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The passage uses antithesis between one and its mate, rich and poor, and few and many.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p531/r14] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The passage uses ellipsis in several places.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p531/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | It repeats key words and meanings: fear, creation, orphan, women, inheritance, and guarding against injustice.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:1#2/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · أبو البقاء | reports | The more evident parse makes كثيرا an adjective of رجالا; Abu al-Baqa says its masculine form follows the semantic sense of رجال as a number, class, or collective, like masculine verb agreement with a feminine collective.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:1#2/r10] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | Another reading is تسلون, with the hamza's vowel transferred to the سِين.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:1#2/r11] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The reciprocal form can mean either asking one another or simply فعل; Abdullah's simple-verb reading supports the latter sense.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:1#2/r12] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · أبو البقاء | reports | Abu al-Baqa explains the preposition on the object by understanding the verb as تتحالفون, since asking itself would take the object directly.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:1#2/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | The example وقال نسوة shows a masculine verb used with the feminine collective نسوة. | mentions 12:30
[SAMIN-DURR:4:1#2/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | Alternatively كثيرا modifies an omitted verbal noun: God dispersed them with a great dispersal; Sibawayh treats comparable forms as accusative circumstantial expressions.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:1#2/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | One answer to why abundance is attached to men alone is that the adjective for women is omitted because the preceding description supplies it: many women.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:1#2/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | A second answer is that public prominence suits men, whereas privacy and concealment better suit women.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:1#2/r6] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The Kufans lighten the سِين by deleting one of the two تاءs for ease; the original is تتساءلون, though grammarians differed over which تاء was deleted.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:1#2/r7] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | The source notes a prior disagreement about whether the first or second تاء was deleted.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:1#2/r8] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Other readers double the سِين by assimilating the تاء of reciprocal form into it because of their close similarity in voicing; ست is cited from سدس.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:1#2/r9] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | Abdullah reads تسألون from the simple triliteral verb سأل.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:1#3/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | Most readers put والأرحام in the accusative, either coordinating it with God's name to mean respect kinship by not severing it, or supplying an implicit قطع; this is specific under general reverence for God.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:1#3/r10] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | Some supply an omitted رب, reading رب الأرحام; Abu al-Baqa says the preceding mention of God already supplies it.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:1#3/r11] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The author answers that God may swear by whatever He chooses, including created things such as the sun, star, and night, although people are forbidden to do so; semantically the verse is not an oath.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:1#3/r12] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | prefers | Because the intended meaning is not an oath, the author prefers coordination with the pronoun and disregards criticism of Hamza's reading, whose high standing precludes transmitting a weak reading.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:1#3/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The author says fearing God means avoiding disobedience, which already includes cutting kinship ties, so this is a specific case under the general command.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:1#3/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | The second accusative parse coordinates kinship with the underlying position of the pronoun in به; Abdullah's reading وبالأرحام supports this.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:1#3/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · أبو البقاء | reports | Abu al-Baqa reads the phrase as exalting God and kinship, since swearing by God honors Him.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:1#3/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | Hamza reads والأرحام in the genitive; one analysis coordinates it with the genitive pronoun in به without repeating the preposition, a construction Basrans reject and previously debated with 2:217. | mentions 2:217
[SAMIN-DURR:4:1#3/r6] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الزجاج | reports | Al-Zajjaj and others criticized Hamza's reading of the genitive coordination.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:1#3/r7] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الفراء | reports | Al-Farra, despite allowing such coordination, calls it ugly and reports Ibrahim's comparison: أسألك بالله والرحم, since Arabs do not coordinate onto a genitive represented by a pronoun.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:1#3/r8] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | A second genitive analysis treats the و as an oath particle and the kinship term as the object of oath, answered by إن الله كان عليكم رقيبا.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:1#3/r9] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | rejects | The oath analysis is weak because the accusative reading and the reading with an explicit preposition point elsewhere, and reports prohibit swearing by anything besides God.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:1#4/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · ابن عطية | reports | In Abdullah's nominative reading, Ibn Atiyya makes والأرحام a subject with the omitted predicate أهل أن توصل, worthy of being joined.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:1#4/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الزمخشري | prefers | Al-Zamakhshari supplies the predicate مما يتقى or مما يتساءل به; the author prefers this because it fits both wording and meaning, unlike Ibn Atiyya's semantic-only fit.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:1#4/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · أبو البقاء | reports | Abu al-Baqa supplies محترمة as the predicate: kinship ties are sacrosanct and their respect is obligatory.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:1#4/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The statement that God is ever watchful over people functions as the reason for the command.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:1#4/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Raqīb is an intensive adjective from raqaba and related forms, meaning God's vigilant preservation or guardianship.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:1#4/r6] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | An anonymous poem uses الرقباء for watchmen, supporting the vigilant sense of raqīb.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:1#4/r7] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Raqīb also names a kind of snake.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:1#4/r8] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Raqīb also names the third arrow in the game of maysir.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:1#4/r9] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The verbal noun irtiqāb means waiting or expectation.

/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | من نفس is an accusative complement of خلقكم, with من marking the starting point; likewise منها زوجها and بث منهما depend on their respective verbs.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:1/r10] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الزمخشري | reports | Al-Zamakhshari limits that direct coordination to an address aimed at the Messenger's contemporaries, who are created from Adam and whose mother Eve was created from him.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:1/r11] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | rejects | The author questions al-Zamakhshari's apparent restriction of this parsing to contemporaries of the Messenger.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:1/r12] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | Some supply an implicit جنس, reading منها as from her kind; this belongs to those who say Eve was not created from Adam but from leftover clay, a view the author rejects.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:1/r13] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | rejects | The view that Eve was created from leftover clay rather than Adam is described as undesirable.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:1/r14] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الزمخشري | reports | A reading has وخالق وباث as active participles; al-Zamakhshari parses them as predicates of an omitted subject, meaning he is creator and disperser.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:1/r15] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The verbs بث and أبث both mean to disperse, one triliteral and the other quadriliteral.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:1/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · ابن أبي عبلة | reports | Ibn Abi ʿAbla reads واحد without feminine تاء; one explanation agrees with the intended meaning, since نفس refers to Adam.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:1/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · ابن أبي عبلة | reports | A second explanation for the reading واحد is that نفس can be masculine or feminine, supported by a poetic example using ثلاثة أنفس.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:1/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | One parse coordinates وخلق with the semantic sense of واحدة, which implies an action: one soul that was single or separate.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:1/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The verb وحد يحد and its verbal nouns mean to be alone or separate, clarifying that first coordination.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:1/r6] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الزمخشري | reports | Al-Zamakhshari posits an omitted verb such as created or originated before وخلق, yielding the sense that humankind was branched from one soul.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:1/r7] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | Al-Zamakhshari and the preceding grammarian posit the omission to preserve the chronological order in which Eve was created before humans.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:1/r8] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | rejects | The author says no such omission is needed, because the conjunction و does not require chronological order.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:1/r9] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | A third parse coordinates وخلق with خلقكم inside the relative clause; و is immaterial because it does not impose order.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v2p206#2/r1] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | God brought forth Adam and Eve’s many descendants and spread them through the world with diverse peoples, traits, colors, and languages, to return to Him at resurrection.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v2p206#2/r2] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · إبراهيم ومجاهد والحسن | reports | Ibrahim, Mujahid, and al-Hasan explain asking one another by God and kinship as saying, ‘I ask you by God and by kinship.’
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v2p206#2/r3] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · الضحاك | reports | Al-Dahhak reads the wording as invoking God by whom people make covenants and pledges.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v2p206#2/r4] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · ابن عباس ومجاهد وعكرمة والحسن والضحاك والربيع | reports | The command concerning kinship means not to sever ties but to honor and maintain them.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v2p206#2/r5] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · بعضهم | reports | Some readers pronounce al-arḥām in the genitive, coordinating it with the pronoun in ‘by Him,’ so people ask by God and kinship.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v2p206#3/r1] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | God watches all deeds and circumstances, as also stated at 85:9. | mentions 85:9
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v2p206#3/r2] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | A sound hadith commands worship with awareness that God sees the worshipper, even when the worshipper does not see Him.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v2p206#3/r3] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | Mentioning humanity’s one father and mother should foster mutual affection and compassion toward the weak.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v2p206#3/r4] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | After Mudar’s poor, scantily clothed delegation arrived, the Prophet recited 4:1 and 59:18 in a sermon, then urged people to give charity. | mentions 59:18
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v2p206#3/r5] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · ابن مسعود | reports | The report of Ibn Mas‘ud’s sermon of need says the Prophet recited three verses, including 4:1.
[BURHAN:v1p260#2/r1] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | The surah order appears divinely fixed, with alphabetic grouping, matching adjacent endings and beginnings, verbal rhythm, and thematic similarity among its reasons.
[BURHAN:v1p260#2/r10] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | Its opening invokes the single soul, spouse, God, and kinship; the surah then treats agreements, property, marriage, inheritance, and prophetic covenants.
[BURHAN:v1p260#2/r9] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | Al-Nisa contains rules for relationships, including God-created kinship and marriage ties and human agreements.
[BURHAN:v1p318/r1] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | The Qurʾān is the revelation given to Muhammad for exposition and inimitability, whereas readings are variations in its written letters or their performance, such as lightening and doubling.
[BURHAN:v1p318/r2] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | Al-Dānī's al-Taysīr is recommended for the seven readings; al-Shāṭibī versified it, Ibn al-Bādhish wrote al-Iqnāʿ, and al-Shahrazūrī's al-Miṣbāḥ covers the ten readings.
[BURHAN:v1p318/r3] BURHAN, d. 794 · الجمهور | reports | The majority regard the seven readings as mass-transmitted, while another view calls them merely well-known.
[BURHAN:v1p318/r4] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | rejects | The objections of al-Mubarrad to Hamza's al-arḥām and miṣrikhī, and of Ibn ʿAṣfūr to Ibn ʿĀmir's reading, do not count against the canonical readings.
[BURHAN:v1p318/r5] BURHAN, d. 794 · أبو شامة | reports | Abū Shāma noted that the documented chains for the seven readings pass from one transmitter to another and do not uniformly meet the conditions of mass transmission at every level.
[BURHAN:v1p318/r6] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | The seven readings are mass-transmitted from their seven imams, though whether that transmission is mass-transmitted all the way back to the Prophet requires qualification.
[BURHAN:v1p318/r7] BURHAN, d. 794 · أبو عمرو بن الحاجب | reports | Ibn al-Ḥājib excludes performance features such as lengthening, imāla, and easing hamza from the claim that the seven readings are mass-transmitted.
[BURHAN:v1p318/r8] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | rejects | The exclusion is weak: lengthening and imāla are certainly mass-transmitted as shared categories, although readers differ over their degree.
[BURHAN:v1p318/r9] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | Readers differ in measured length: Hamza and Warsh use six units, with reports of five or four; ʿĀṣim uses three, al-Kisāʾī two and a half, Qālūn two, and al-Sūsī one and a half.
[BURHAN:v1p321/r1] BURHAN, d. 794 · ابن الحاجب | reports | Ibn al-Ḥājib explains that an interrogative hamza is followed by a long vowel before an open wasl hamza to avoid confusing a question with a statement, as in āl-ḥasanu ʿindak.
[BURHAN:v1p321/r2] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | Some Arabs soften the wasl hamza between two pronunciations; readers transmit both forms, though the lengthened form is standard, and the Uthmanic spelling of a second hamza as wāw signals the softened form. | mentions 3:15
[BURHAN:v1p321/r3] BURHAN, d. 794 · الشاطبي | reports | For two hamzas in separate words with matching vowels, Abū ʿAmr drops the first according to al-Shāṭibī; another view says the second is dropped, as in jāʾa ajaluhum. | mentions 10:49
[BURHAN:v1p321/r4] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | In the open-hamza case, Nāfiʿ through Qālūn and Ibn Kathīr through al-Bazzī also transmit dropping a hamza; Qunbul transmits its deletion within the single word shirkāʾī. | mentions 6:22
[BURHAN:v1p321/r5] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | Qurʾānic readings are fixed by transmission, not selected through grammarians' taste or eloquent reasoning; this rejects al-Zamakhsharī's criticism of Hamza's genitive al-arḥām and other disputed readings.
[BURHAN:v1p366/r3] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | Stops at an object, a specifying circumstantial phrase, or an exception that changes meaning fall between the tighter and looser attachment classes; examples include مسغبة, قليلا, مصيرا, واحدة, زوجها, and نذيرا.
[BURHAN:v2p120/r10] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | The grammarians may only have meant that Hamza's reading is sound and eloquent though another reading is more eloquent; not every Qurʾānic expression must be at the highest degree.
[BURHAN:v2p120/r9] BURHAN, d. 794 · أبو بصر بن القشيري | rejects | He argues that rejecting a reading established from the Prophet is perilous; Arabic is learned from the Prophet, whose eloquence is beyond doubt, rather than from language authorities who criticize it.
[BURHAN:v2p301/r3] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | One purpose of kināya is to draw attention to divine power: creating humanity from one soul alludes to Adam.
[BURHAN:v2p466/r2] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | Scholars differ whether a specific member stated after a general term was already included; the added mention can be emphatic, and al-Rūyānī reports a related two-view dispute in a bequest case.
[BURHAN:v2p466/r3] BURHAN, d. 794 · الروياني | reports | Al-Rūyānī reports two views on whether a poor Zayd receives both a named dinar and a share of a bequest to the poor; the stronger view gives him only the dinar be

[BURHAN:v2p466/r5] BURHAN, d. 794 · الزمخشري | reports | Al-Zamakhsharī sometimes allows a later conjunct to attach either to the first conjunct or to the nearer preceding phrase.
[BURHAN:v2p466/r6] BURHAN, d. 794 · الزمخشري | reports | Al-Zamakhsharī attaches mukhrij al-mayyit to fāliq rather than yukh’rij, avoiding coordination of a noun with a verb; Ibn Mālik disagrees and offers another analysis. | mentions 6:95
[BURHAN:v2p466/r7] BURHAN, d. 794 · الزمخشري | reports | Al-Zamakhsharī reads al-malāʾikah in the phrase about God's coming as coordinated with Allah, linking it to the eternal decree. | mentions 2:210
[BURHAN:v2p466/r8] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | If yā ayyuhā al-nās is universal, wa-khalaqa minhā zawjahā coordinates with an omitted verb, meaning He originated and brought her into being; if addressed to Meccans, khalaqa coordinates with khalaqakum, avoiding repetition.
[BURHAN:v3p106/r1] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | Arabic can delete the nun of a dual or plural while its grammatical trace remains; the reading al-muqīmī al-ṣalāh illustrates this, as do shortened forms in extended relative clauses. | mentions 4:162
[BURHAN:v3p106/r2] BURHAN, d. 794 · الأخفش | reports | Al-Muʾarrij al-Sadūsī asked al-Akhfash why ya is omitted in wa-l-layli idhā yasri; the answer was that Arabs reduce letters when a word is shifted from its ordinary sense, since night is traveled through rather than traveling. | mentions 89:4, 19:28
[BURHAN:v3p106/r3] BURHAN, d. 794 · الرماني | reports | Al-Rummānī explains final ya deletion as preserving the verse ending: endings are treated as if paused, like poetic rhyme. | mentions 93:3, 89:4
[BURHAN:v3p106/r4] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | In Moses' answer to Pharaoh, the subjects before the repeated Lord descriptions are omitted; Moses magnifies Pharaoh's audacity and points instead to God's distinctive acts, establishing that God has no likeness. | mentions 26:23, 26:24, 26:28
[BURHAN:v3p106/r5] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | The subject is omitted in ṣummun bukmun ʿumyun, with the pronoun hum understood, to spare the tongue from stating it explicitly. | mentions 2:18
[BURHAN:v3p106/r6] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | Some divine descriptions admit no other implicit subject: ʿālim al-ghayb and faʿʿāl li-mā yurīd are understood of God. | mentions 6:73, 11:107
[BURHAN:v3p106/r7] BURHAN, d. 794 · الزمخشري | reports | When an omitted element is so familiar that stating it adds nothing, contextual evidence can speak more clearly than words; al-Zamakhsharī applies this to Hamza's reading, where the preposition before al-arḥām is understood from the preceding phrase.
[BURHAN:v3p106/r8] BURHAN, d. 794 · الفارسي | reports | Al-Fārisī explains the genitive al-arḥām with an elided repeated preposition, wa-bi-l-arḥām, recoverable from the preceding genitive pronoun.
[BURHAN:v3p111/r1] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | An omission must be indicated by wording or context; otherwise the expression becomes unintelligible or an inelegant riddle. What remains must guide the reader to what was omitted.
[BURHAN:v3p111/r2] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | Inflection can signal an omitted governor: on the accusative reading of al-arḥām, an understood command such as wa-iḥfaẓū al-arḥām supplies its case.
[BURHAN:v3p111/r3] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | Meaning and contextual knowledge can require an omitted object; the broad expression yaḥillu wa-yarbiṭu means that someone manages affairs and has full discretion.
[BURHAN:v3p111/r4] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | Syntax can reveal omissions: lā uqsim is understood as la-anā uqsim because a present-tense act is not sworn by, while tafʾat tadhkuru Yūsuf requires a negative lā. | mentions 75:1, 12:85, 64:7
[BURHAN:v3p111/r5] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | A single construction may allow multiple implied comparisons; one reading of afaman zuyyina lahu says it contrasts the beautified sinner with someone whose evil deed was not beautified. | mentions 35:8
[BURHAN:v3p252/r1] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | The text commonly gives precedence to men as a mark of their distinction, as in its mention of many men and women. | mentions 33:35, 53:21
[BURHAN:v3p252/r2] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | Precedence can mark distinctions in prophethood, freedom, reason, faith, knowledge, life, and the nobility of what is known; the cited examples place the more honored item first. | mentions 7:87, 25:61, 43:32, 6:122, 39:9, 35:19, 3:18, 57:17, 35:22, 6:73
[BURHAN:v3p252/r3] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | When daughters are named first in the gift of children, the order compensates them as a vulnerable group; the definiteness used for sons compensates them for losing precedence. | mentions 42:49
[BURHAN:v3p252/r4] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | reports | Another possible reason for naming daughters first is to show that all creation follows God's will rather than human preference. | mentions 42:49
[BURHAN:v3p252/r5] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | Other orderings follow causal or temporal priority: livestock precede people as the cause, and death precedes life because it existed earlier. | mentions 80:32, 67:2
[BURHAN:v3p252/r6] BURHAN, d. 794 · القرطبي | reports | Al-Qurṭubī reports an unusual dispute over whether a free person is more noble than an enslaved person and directs readers to the discussion in his Sūrat al-Nisāʾ commentary. | mentions 2:178
[BURHAN:v3p252/r7] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | The unseen is nobler than what is witnessed, explaining the order in ʿālim al-ghayb wa-l-shahādah. | mentions 6:73
[BURHAN:v3p366/r1] BURHAN, d. 794 · أبو البقاء | reports | Abu al-Baqa explains the feminine ذائقة in كل نفس ذائقة الموت by following the feminine sense of كل, as each soul means a set of souls.
[BURHAN:v3p366/r2] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | rejects | Zarkashi rejects Abu al-Baqa's analysis: when كل is annexed to an indefinite noun, agreement should follow the noun, not كل.
[BURHAN:v4p113/r1] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | Conjunction may be omitted when the first of two statements already calls for the second; each then sounds like an independent statement while the mind still links them.
[BURHAN:v4p113/r10] BURHAN, d. 794 · الكوفيون | reports | The Kufans say a preposition need not be repeated before a conjunct on a genitive pronoun, citing Hamza's genitive reading al-arḥām; an alternative parses it as an oath.
[BURHAN:v4p113/r2] BURHAN, d. 794 · الجمهور | reports | Most grammarians require a separator before coordinating onto an independent nominative pronoun; the examples emphasize the pronoun before adding the conjunct. | mentions 7:27, 5:24, 2:35
[BURHAN:v4p113/r3] BURHAN, d. 794 · ابن مالك | reports | Ibn Mālik treats اسكن أنت وزوجك as coordination of clauses, supplying an implicit wa-li-taskun zawjuka rather than coordinating onto the pronoun. | mentions 2:35
[BURHAN:v4p113/r4] BURHAN, d. 794 · الزمخشري | reports | On the reading with an open wāw, al-Zamakhsharī analyzes aw ābāʾunā in the resurrection question as a conjunct on the pronoun, with the hamza as separator. | mentions 37:16
[BURHAN:v4p113/r5] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | rejects | The proposed analysis of aw ābāʾunā is challenged because an interrogative hamza does not govern an isolated noun. | mentions 37:16
[BURHAN:v4p113/r6] BURHAN, d. 794 · الفارسي | reports | Al-Fārisī gives mā ashraknā wa-lā ābāʾunā as another coordination example; Ibn al-Dahhān instead parses wa-lā ābāʾunā as a subject with an implicit predicate, ashrakū. | mentions 6:148
[BURHAN:v4p113/r7] BURHAN, d. 794 · الكوفيون | reports | The Kufans allow coordination onto a pronoun without an intervening separator, citing wa-alladhīna hādū wa-l-ṣābiʾūn. | mentions 5:69

[ALUSI-FULL:v4p180/r8] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · الصادق | reports | A long report in Ibn Babawayh’s al-Tawhid quotes al-Sadiq saying God created a million Adams and that this humanity is the last of them.

[ALUSI-FULL:v4p181/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | rejects | The author rejects as neither sound creed nor certainty the claim that a universal soul judges individual souls every seven thousand years and that the Hour follows the thousandth resurrection.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p181/r10] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | rejects | The author rejects the houri view because no Quranic verse or hadith even hints at it; if houris were made from Paradise saffron, Eve would differ in kind from Adam, and if from Adam’s substance, the claim collapses into Abu Muslim’s position.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p181/r11] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | rejects | The author rejects Abu Muslim’s view because then humanity would come from two souls instead of the single soul stated here, and it conflicts with authentic Prophetic reports; this also undermines the houri view.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p181/r2] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | ربكم and خلقكم address those commanded; extending them to earlier nations while the earlier address excluded them needlessly splits the syntax, since God’s lordship and creation of the addressees already encompass their ancestors.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p181/r3] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Mentioning the addressees’ creation through Adam and their intervening parents also implicitly recognizes all those ancestral links, as does mentioning God’s lordship over them.

[ALUSI-FULL:v4p181/r7] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · أبو مسلم | reports | Abu Muslim denies that Eve was created from Adam’s rib, arguing that God could create her from dust and interpreting منها as “of the same kind,” like the phrase in 16:72. | mentions 16:72
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p181/r8] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | Some agree with Abu Muslim, saying the rib interpretation would mean Adam had intercourse with part of himself, which they find repugnant.

[ALUSI-FULL:v4p182#2/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The preceding discussion suggests this manner of creation was unique to Adam and Eve rather than other animal pairs, but the author has found no fully satisfying evidence on that question.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p182#2/r2] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · ابن عمر | reports | Ibn ʿUmar reports that Iblis's wife was created from his left rear rib; al-Ḍaḥḥāk explains the relevant term as the shortest ribs of the side.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p182#2/r3] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The verse mentions the addressees' creation first because that reminder more directly prompts obedience; fronting “from it” emphasizes Adam as Eve's origin and creates suspense, while “spouse” prepares for reproduction.

[ALUSI-FULL:v4p183#2/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Calling on one another by God in supplication and entreaty itself calls for fearing violation of His commands and prohibitions.

[ALUSI-FULL:v4p183#2/r4] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | One accusative analysis coordinates “kinship” with the grammatical position of “by Him”; it is supported by the reading “by Him and by kinship,” and reports that people paired kinship with God in pleas, as Mujāhid relates.
